MeerKAT Telescope Extraordinary

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Meerkat is now transmitting images of the highest quality of anywhere in the world and we are only half way through the erection.

37 antenna’s are standing tall at the Losberg site in the Karoo…no mean feat 16 months ago had 16 only..these were up and running and producing the very first images of the Universe

This telescope is now the best science instrument in the world it is producing the most close and clear of galaxies never before seen.


Further information:
Over 1 300 galaxies can now be seen in the distant Universe compared with 70 known that could be seen before. We are seeing distant galaxies close up…massive black holes at their centre
Seeing galaxies approximately 200 million light years away where hydrogen gas is being used up to form stars in large numbers.
The images were taken in a small part of the sky comprising 0.01% of the entire celestial sphere

This is the first remarkable scientific milestone reached by MeerKAT…which upon completion will be integrated in the international SKA.

Huge milestones…SA team comprised of more than 200 scientists engineers and technicians, in co operation with industry local and international universities and institutions designed the technology and systems for MeerKAT

Dr Fernando Camilo former research scientist at Columbia University, is chief scientist blown away by the images and how much has been accomplished in South African Radio astronomy over the past decade…hi highly regarded around for his work in this fi

Press Release:


MeerKAT
Just 16 months ago, the MeerKAT Radio Telescope at the Losberg site in the Karoo, had only 16 antennas that produced images of galaxies millions of light years
away. Now, with 32 antennas standing tall, the MeerKAT will be able to transmit high quality, never before seen images of these galaxies in the distant universe. Carte
Blanche explores.

Script:


MeerKAT

V/O 11 sec
Now, for the first time, galaxies, millions of light years away can be seen in high quality definition…This is a South African scientific first.

Link: This is the MeerKAT radio telescope the largest of its kind in the Southern Hemisphere it currently consists of 32 integrated antenna but by the time its finished there will be 64 and when you consider the extraordinary detail of the information its already capturing who know what secrets it might yet reveal about our universe

Fernando: When you build instruments of this nature deliver some questions and new questions pop up and along the way may learn something entirely unexpected

V/O 12 sec
Dr Fernando Camilo is renowned in the field of astrophysics, he came on board last year, when Meerkat had completed 16 dishes of their telescope, it’s first scientific milestone.

Fernando: No body really knew how good it was going to be and it was on the front page of the New York Times it just took world by surprise.

V/O 14 sec NB JOHN WE HAVE EXTENDED THE TIME ON THIS sO DIFF FROM YOUR WE TRANSFER COPY

This was the previous best image of our distant galaxies from a radio telescope. PAUSE With MeerKAT’s 16 antenna telescope the image of the same area of the sky comes sharply into focus.

John: With the image that was provided by the 16 dishes you were able to identify 1300 galaxies in one part of the sky.
Fernando: This image that you see here is about 1% of the area of the entire first light image it spans an area that is a bit bigger than the moon there are close to 1500 galaxies that we detected and indeed previously only 70 galaxies.

V/O 13 sec
As of Thursday MeerKAT’s 32 antennas are fully integrated and operational and we will now be able to not only view our distant galaxies as never before, but start doing real science.

Fernando: It will be by far the best the best science instrument of it’s kind in the whole Southern Hemisphere and in certain aspect it will be the best in the world It will allow us to make images of the radio sky of galaxies of stars with unprecedented sensitivity.

John Are you excited prospects SKA deliver
Fernando: We have some key questions address also my development of galaxies and gravitational waves…pulsar measure g tools…literally things we cannot conceive of today

John: Seeing you walk around this magnificent facility you look incredibly proud?
Fernando: Well I do I feel proud of the team that’s built this facility I myself only arrived a year ago 10 years ago there was a handful of radio astronomers in South Africa people would have laughed at this world class instrument being here a decade later it’s astonishing.

V/O 16 and a half sec
Its here in the Northern Cape, about 800 kilometres from Cape Town, deep in the Karoo that is the site for the Square Kilometre Array or SKA… telescope. The MeerKAT telescope is the stepping stone to what will eventually form SKA.

V/O 9 sec
We won the international site bid to co – host SKA with Australia in 2012…when completed It will be the world’s largest telescope.

Link: This is where it all started an array of radio telescopes known as Kat 7 the success of this project mapped the way forward for what is known as MeerKAT or quiet literally more KAT

LINK
A popular assumption is that telescopes always look at at space from their position here on earth but radio telescopes consistently collect radio frequencies that bombard earth from outer space.

V/O 9 sec
As Maintenance Manager it’s Sizwe Seranyane’s job to ensure that these receivers – each weighing 42 tons - are in good working order.

John: It’s interesting that they are big and in some ways quiet cumbersome but they are in some ways quiet fragile and very sensitive as well.
Siswe: You want to have as large as you can the collecting surface, these work in an array so linked together they are they are one giant telescope

V/O 6 and a half sec
KAT 7, was built to observe near by galaxies, its images of the distant universe are poor.

Fernando: MeerKAT is an entirely different beast so what you see here now is an image with four dishes from Meerkat, with the same patch of SKY.
John: So then 4 dishes become 16 and what does that do to the image?
Fernando: So when we put 16 Meerkat dishes together you get this altogether and really beautiful image, there’s a black hole connected by two jets, this image tells you what you really want to know.

V/O 14 sec
The secret behind the success of MeerKAT’s images of our universe is an age old mathematical problem solved by an unlikely algorithm … working in this field is the brilliant Dr Sphesihle Makhatini

Dr Sphesihle Makhathini - Data Scientist  (SKA South Africa) 

Sphe: When I had the opportunity to join the project I couldn’t say no.

V/O 9 sec
Sphe’s still technically a student at Rhodes, but an opportunity like this is a jumpstart for someone at the beginning of their science career.

John: In layman’s terms can you describe exactly what your job entails?
Sphe: What we do is take a picture of the sky there’s a lot of like complexity in doing that because for 1…not taking a picture of the full sky because you only have dishes on some parts of the ground, so there is missing information that we don’t get so Part 1 we actually try to write algorithms to fill in these gaps. A simple example for me would be for me my eyes don’t work properly so if I don’t have my glasses cant see exactly what is happening but these lenses will correct for those errors

Isabella: Growing up in the rural areas where you don’t have much to do///the night sky is phenomenal and you get to look at the stars and you ask yourself what are those things why are they so small, why do I always see them but sometimes I see that they are shifting why do they do that, so those type of questions are the questions that got me into doing astronomy.

V/O 10 and a half sec
Isabella Rammala joined SKA under their young professionals development programme, she’s doing her post graduate studies part time while working on MeerKAT

Isabella: When I was in high school I did not even know where I am going to study astronomy I didn’t have access to the internet, I asked people they had never heard of astronomy before so it was only luck that I got this prospectus from Free State and their was this thing called astrophysics.

V/O 4 and a half sec
And it’s not just our scientists who are expanding their horizons.

Siswe: We had to come up with ways to ensure that we train up local people.
John: It is a Good News Story
Siswe: To me it is because you can see the changes in peoples lives my curiosity has since changed I look up I will soon be starting with my own observations I would like to start with Jupiter. I am inspired by the project in total

LINK: Most scientific instruments are limited by their own functionality in other words the work of the scientists is confined by what that instrument has been designed to do but the MeerKAT and SKA will be different because they have been designed to answer questions that have not even be posed yet

Fernando: If we are having this conversation 10 years from now I am sure we will be talking about discoveries of MeerKAt that we can not conceive of today.
John One of the major scientific questions is if there is life out there?
Fernando:. The current plan is to have MeerKAT used to search for extra terrestrial intelligence there could well be a planet in the line of sight in the distant galaxy we will be listening for artificial signals from potential intelligent life.

LINK
This collection of wire mesh pvc and wooden poles might not look like much but it is in fact a sensitive scientific instrument known as the HERA telescope it’s a collaboration between universities in the USA UK and SA and is a good example of the international collaboration that also characterises the MeerKAT project

Rob : The HERA looks for a period when the period when very first stars switched on and if you see that that’s Nobel prize
John: So possible Nobel prize for something that is made of PVC and wire mesh?
Rob: Yes absolutely …what it proves is if you show you are committed to excellence and you have the right attitude and you put the right infrastructure in place you you can attract things you don’t even think of.
Fernando: People forget that when you look through a telescope you are really looking through a time machine your looking back in time. it takes light millions and billions of years to travel from these distant galaxies so the further away you’re looking the further back in time you’re looking you are seeing the universe how it was.

LINK : Its remarkable to consider that this massive investment in infrastructure and human capital an investment that will reshape this part of the Karoo is really being done for one purpose to try and figure out our place in the Universe

V/O 12 sec
A quest not unlike the one man has been on since the beginning of time, a quest the San feel a connection with…At the launch of MeerKAT’s 32 dishes they blessed the site..

Rob I think we should never lose our roots in science which is the wonder of the cosmos and whether that wonder is in the traditional way with the San person standing up and looking at the stars or from a modern cosmologist the basic human instinct of wonder and wanting to know that’s the same.
